lessons.title: Tessellation: shapes that fit together
objectives: Design a tessellating tile by changing a square

keywords.def: a pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps or overlaps
a flat shape repeated to cover a surface
to slide a shape without turning it

starter: Bismillah. How many petals has our six-petal flower?
Name a shape that has four equal sides.

teach.heading: What is tessellation?
teach.note: Show a tiled floor photo. Ask why a gap would be a problem. Pupils need squared paper or plain paper, ruler, pencil, scissors (with adult), crayons.

teach.heading: Which shapes tessellate?
bullets: Regular hexagons do; circles do not
teach.note: Ask why circles leave gaps. Misconception: any shape tessellates. Test with paper cutouts.

teach.heading: Escher and the Alhambra
bullets: M. C. Escher was a Dutch artist
He studied tiles at the Alhambra in Spain
He changed shapes to make new tessellations
teach.note: Keep this brief and use only Escher's non-figurative pieces if shown; avoid animals or people. The Alhambra is a medieval palace in Granada.

teach.heading: Changing a square
bullets: Cut a shape from one side
Slide it to the opposite side
Tape it in place to make a new tile
teach.note: Model with paper: cut a notch from the left, slide it to the right and tape. The area stays the same, so the tile still fits.

teach.heading: Tracing the tile
bullets: Slide it across and trace again
teach.note: Check pupils slide, not rotate, for this tile type.

practice: Which of these shapes tessellates: circle, square, star?
Name one place you see tessellation.
independent: Draw squares, triangles and hexagons side by side; which leave gaps?
Draw four copies of a square tile with a notch and slide to fit them.
exit: Make your own tessellating tile from a square and trace it nine times.
Colour it with two or three colours.
lessons.send: Spot and sketch a tessellation at home, such as floor tiles or a pattern.

lessons.title: One-point perspective: a corridor of arches
objectives: Explain vanishing point and horizon line
Draw a corridor in one-point perspective
Add arches that get smaller with distance

keywords.def: a way of drawing that makes flat paper look three-dimensional
the line where the ground seems to meet the sky
the point where parallel lines seem to meet
a light line used to help draw

starter: Name the three layers of a landscape.

teach.heading: Why do things look smaller?
bullets: That meeting point is the vanishing point
teach.note: Show a photo of a long road or corridor. Ask where the lines meet. Pupils need paper, pencil, a ruler.

teach.heading: Setting up
bullets: Draw a horizon line across the page
Put a dot in the middle: the vanishing point
Draw a rectangle at the front
teach.note: Model with the ruler. Use light pencil. Misconception: vanishing point is at the bottom of the page; it must be on the horizon.

teach.heading: Drawing the corridor
bullets: Draw lines from the corners to the dot
Stop where you want the end wall
Draw the back wall as a smaller rectangle
teach.note: Walk through slowly. Pupils can check by laying the ruler from each corner to the dot.

teach.heading: Arches that shrink
bullets: Draw one big arch at the front
Draw smaller arches along the walls
Aim lines for the vanishing point
teach.note: Arches are architectural and fit our guidelines. Keep sizes shrinking evenly.

teach.heading: Shading for depth
bullets: Shade walls darker near the front
teach.note: Self-check: do all lines point at the dot? Partners share on camera.

practice: Where do railway lines seem to meet?
independent: Draw a horizon line, vanishing point and a front rectangle.
Draw guidelines from the corners to the vanishing point.
exit: Complete a corridor with at least four arches getting smaller.
homework: Why do arches at the back look smaller?
lessons.send: Draw a corridor, street or room you know in one-point perspective.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Colour in landscapes, mixed media and a model building (Ground-Breaking Greeks)
lessons.title: Tints, shades and tones
lessons.bigQuestion: How many different greens can you see out of a window? Where do they all come from?
objectives: To understand how to mix tints, shades and tones of a colour to show light and depth
successCriteria: All: mix a tint and a shade
Most: mix tones by adding grey
Some: make a colour chart of three colours in tints, tones and shades
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at colour in creation

hook.text: How many different greens can you see out of a window? Where do they all come from?
hook.a: Many: light, shadow and distance change the same hue into tints, shades and tones.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do you not see that Allah sends down rain from the sky, and We produce thereby fruits of varying colors? And in the mountains are tracts, white and red of varying shades and [some] extremely black.' (Fatir 35:27).

teach.heading: Mixing safely
bullets: Add dark to light, a little at a time

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

practice.a: Two lighter greens, one lighter than the other.
practice.model: I do: green, then add a little white; then more white for a lighter tint.

independent.q: Paint a colour chart of three hues with two tints, two shades and one tone each; label them.
independent.model: The teacher paints the blue row.

independent.q: Extend: find two of your colours in a landscape photo.

exit.q: A tint is a colour plus ...
Back to our ponder: How many different greens can you see out of a window? Where do they all come from?
exit.a: Many: light, shadow and distance change the same hue into tints, shades and tones.

lessons.homework: Find three tints and three shades in your home.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Colour in landscapes, mixed media and a model building (Ground-Breaking Greeks)
lessons.title: A Mediterranean landscape
lessons.bigQuestion: Greece and many Muslim lands share the same sea. What colours would you expect in a Mediterranean coast?
objectives: To understand how to use tints, shades and tones to paint a landscape with foreground, middle ground and background
successCriteria: Most: use lighter tints for the background
Some: add detail in the foreground for depth
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and history: Ancient Greece and the Mediterranean
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the Mediterranean shared by many civilisations

keywords.def: where land or sea meets the sky

hook.text: Greece and many Muslim lands share the same sea. What colours would you expect in a Mediterranean coast?
hook.a: Deep blues and turquoises in the sea, white buildings, olive greens, warm ochre hills.

starter.q: A tone is a colour plus ...

starter.a: where sky meets land or sea
options: where sky meets land or sea

misconception.wrong: Painting the far hills as dark as the near rocks
misconception.right: Far is paler and bluer; near is darker with detail

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Which part should have the most detail?

practice.a: A strip from pale sky to deep sea blue.
practice.model: I do: pale tint at the top, add more blue as I go down, darker at the bottom.

independent.q: Paint a Mediterranean coast or hillside (no people) with three grounds; photograph and upload.
independent.model: The teacher paints the sky and horizon on camera.

independent.q: Extend: add an olive tree in the foreground with shades.
independent.a: An olive tree with light and dark greens.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Greece and many Muslim lands share the same sea. What colours would you expect in a Mediterranean coast?
exit.a: Deep blues and turquoises in the sea, white buildings, olive greens, warm ochre hills.

lessons.homework: Finish your landscape and upload it.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Colour in landscapes, mixed media and a model building (Ground-Breaking Greeks)
lessons.title: DT: designing a building with columns, arches and a dome
lessons.bigQuestion: Ancient Greeks built with columns; later Muslim architects built many arches and domes. Why might curves be strong?
objectives: To understand how columns, arches and domes work and design a model building that uses them
successCriteria: Most: sketch and label a front view
Some: choose materials and explain why

keywords.def: a curved structure over an opening

hook.text: Ancient Greeks built with columns; later Muslim architects built many arches and domes. Why might curves be strong?
hook.a: Curves spread the weight down and outwards, so arches and domes can span wide spaces.

islamicLink.text: Muslim architects developed the pointed arch and great domes, for example the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (completed 691 CE) and the arches of the Great Mosque of Cordoba.

starter.q: Name one colour in your landscape.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

practice.q: Label the features on the photo of the Parthenon.
practice.model: I do: these tall supports are columns; the triangle on top is a pediment.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: design your building: front view with at least two features, labels, sizes and materials.
independent.a: A labelled design with features and materials.
independent.model: The teacher designs a front with two columns and an arch.

independent.q: Extend: explain why you chose your materials.
independent.a: Tubes for columns because they are strong and round.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Ancient Greeks built with columns; later Muslim architects built many arches and domes. Why might curves be strong?
exit.a: Curves spread the weight down and outwards, so arches and domes can span wide spaces.

lessons.homework: Collect cardboard tubes, boxes and card for the build.

lessons.title: Mixed media: Greek key and Islamic geometric borders (condensed)
lessons.bigQuestion: The Greek key and Islamic star patterns both repeat. Why do people love repeating patterns?
objectives: To understand how to layer torn paper and texture to make a mixed-media border inspired by Greek and Islamic patterns
successCriteria: All: tear and layer paper to make texture
Most: make a repeating Greek key or geometric border
Some: combine paint and paper in one design
lessons.smsc: Cultural: shared love of pattern across civilisations

keywords.def: using more than one material in one artwork
one material on top of another

hook.text: The Greek key and Islamic star patterns both repeat. Why do people love repeating patterns?
hook.a: They feel ordered and calm; repetition creates rhythm and balance.

teach.heading: Mixed media steps
teach.note: Condensed EXTENSION lesson in the short week of 5 Apr.
cycle: Tear paper for a textured background

teach.heading: Repeat accurately
bullets: Use a ruler and squared paper

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

practice.q: Draw one unit of the Greek key on squared paper.
practice.a: A squared spiral unit 4 squares wide.
practice.model: I do: along 4, up 3, back 2, down 1, along 1... then repeat the unit.

independent.q: Make a mixed-media border (A4 strip): torn-paper background plus a Greek key or geometric repeat; photograph and upload.
independent.a: A layered border with an accurate repeat.
independent.model: The teacher tears and layers the background on camera.

independent.q: Extend: add a second material (tissue or foil) to the pattern.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: The Greek key and Islamic star patterns both repeat. Why do people love repeating patterns?
exit.a: They feel ordered and calm; repetition creates rhythm and balance.

lessons.homework: Finish the border; bring card and tubes for the build.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Colour in landscapes, mixed media and a model building (Ground-Breaking Greeks)
lessons.title: DT: making the model building
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes a tall model wobbly, and how could you fix it?
objectives: To understand how to build a stable model from card and tubes with strong joins
successCriteria: All: build walls and columns that stand
Most: make an arch or dome
Some: test stability and strengthen weak joins
lessons.smsc: Moral: perseverance and teamwork at home

keywords.def: something built to stand and hold weight

hook.text: What makes a tall model wobbly, and how could you fix it?
hook.a: A small base and weak joins; widen the base, use tabs and triangles.

starter.q: Which features are in your design?
A wide base makes a model ...

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: A triangle brace makes a corner ...

practice.q: Make one tab join between two pieces of card.
practice.a: A folded and glued tab holding two pieces at a right angle.
practice.model: I do: fold 1 cm flap, glue, press against the other piece, hold for 30 seconds.

independent.q: Build your model from your design (finish at home), test stability and strengthen weak points; photograph and upload.
independent.a: A standing model with at least one arch or dome.
independent.model: The teacher builds two columns and an arch on camera.

independent.q: Extend: record one fix you made after testing.
independent.a: For example: added a triangle brace.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: What makes a tall model wobbly, and how could you fix it?
exit.a: A small base and weak joins; widen the base, use tabs and triangles.

lessons.title: Evaluate and class gallery
lessons.bigQuestion: How should we give feedback to make someone want to keep improving?
objectives: To understand how to evaluate my landscape and model against the success criteria and give kind feedback
successCriteria: All: say whether my work met the criteria
Most: give evidence from my work
Some: suggest improvements and explain them

keywords.def: what the work had to do

hook.text: How should we give feedback to make someone want to keep improving?
hook.a: Kindly, specifically: one strength and one helpful idea.

head: Work
Criteria
rows: Features from design; stands up; neat joins

teach.heading: Evaluation frame
cycle: It did not fully meet ... because ...

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Which is the most helpful feedback?
options: 'The arch is neat; a wider base would stop the wobble'
check.why: Specific strength plus a helpful idea.

practice.q: Write one evaluation sentence for your landscape.
practice.a: 'My background is paler than my foreground, so it shows depth.'
practice.model: I do: criterion + evidence: 'I used three tints in the sky, so it fades to the horizon.'

independent.q: Pupil PDF: evaluate both pieces with the frame; then gallery: hold work to the camera and give a star and a wish to two classmates.
independent.a: Two evaluations and two peer comments.
independent.model: The teacher evaluates a sample model.

independent.q: Extend: which skill improved most this half term?

exit.q: Back to our ponder: How should we give feedback to make someone want to keep improving?
exit.a: Kindly, specifically: one strength and one helpful idea.

lessons.homework: Share your work with your family and explain one thing you learned.
